props.title: The Conformist

sections.content: The Conformist (1970) stands as Bernardo Bertolucci's masterpiece of political and psychological cinema, revolutionizing how films could explore fascism through individual psychology. The story of Marcello Clerici, a man desperate to be "normal" in Mussolini's Italy, became a blueprint for examining authoritarianism through visual style. Bertolucci and cinematographer Vittorio Storaro created a groundbreaking aesthetic that influenced everything from The Godfather (1972) to Blade Runner (1982) - using Art Deco architecture, shadows, and precise geometric framing to show how fascism seduces through beauty while crushing the soul.

sections.content: The film's influence on American cinema cannot be overstated. Taxi Driver (1976) and Raging Bull (1980) drew from its psychological complexity and visual sophistication. Scorsese has cited it as a major influence, particularly in how Bertolucci used architecture and movement to externalize internal states. The film's famous dancing scene, where fascist geometry transforms into sensual curves, demonstrated how political ideas could be expressed purely through visual style.

Beyond its technical innovations, The Conformist pioneered a new way of depicting political extremism through character psychology. This approach influenced later films like The Lives of Others (2006) and In the Name of the Father (1993), which similarly explored how political systems corrupt individual souls. Bertolucci's genius was showing fascism not as an abstract force but as something that grows from human weakness and desire for acceptance. SUBHEAD: Visual Innovation and Legacy

sections.content: The film's revolutionary use of color and composition created a template for neo-noir that resonates today. Films like Drive (2011) and The American (2010) clearly draw from Storaro's pioneering work. The Conformist's famous "leaves scene" - where autumn leaves swirl around a political assassination - showed how natural beauty could be used to heighten moral horror, influencing sequences in The Godfather Part II (1974) and Road to Perdition (2002).
